skills.name: Multi-Step Sequential Execution
skills.description: Complete all requested sub-tasks in a single conversation without stopping early. When a user asks for N actions (e.g., cancel multiple reservations, modify multiple items, update address AND change item), the agent must execute every action in sequence rather than completing only the first one or two. This requires tracking which sub-tasks have been done, which remain, and continuing until all are finished before summarizing to the user.
skills.reasoning: A-18 required downgrading multiple reservations (JG7FMM, 2FBBAH, X7BYG1, EQ1G6C, BOH180) but the agent only updated one. A-41 was asked to cancel all of a user's upcoming reservations but missed several (failed to look up UDMOP1, XAZ3C0, LU15PA, MSJ4OA, I6M8JQ, 4XGCCM). R-71 and R-72 both needed an address change plus item modification; the agent only completed the item modification and missed the address update. R-109 and R-110 similarly required address + item changes across two orders but only one was completed. The pattern is consistent: agent announces completion after the first successful tool call rather than continuing through all queued sub-tasks.

skills.name: Precise Tool Argument Construction
skills.description: When calling a tool, accurately construct every parameter from the data already retrieved. This includes: selecting the exact flight number or item ID the user specified (not a similar one), computing the correct total price before submitting a payment, choosing the right cabin class and date, and passing the correct payment method ID. Errors here cause the tool to either fail outright or silently commit the wrong state to the database.
skills.reasoning: A-20 repeatedly submitted payment amounts that did not add up to the flight price (submitted 350 when total was 255, then 152, then finally correct). A-25 computed the wrong total price by including membership perks as a cost. A-8 passed the wrong payment split to book_reservation. In retail, R-44 computed a wrong price difference and selected the wrong item ID. R-6/R-7/R-8 consistently called exchange with the wrong new_item_id for the desk lamp variant. R-46/R-47 searched with malformed order IDs (#9502126 vs #W9502126) and computed incorrect refund totals. In airline, A-15 and A-16 both selected the wrong flight combination from the search results instead of the one the user specified.

skills.name: Policy and Constraint Enforcement
skills.description: Apply domain rules strictly regardless of user pressure or sympathetic framing. Key rules include: basic economy flights cannot be modified; refunds must go to the original payment method; compensation certificates require documented qualifying events at the correct amount; cancellations of non-refundable tickets should be declined; and exchanges can only be performed on delivered orders (not pending). The agent must verify claimed facts (e.g., user claiming they bought insurance) against actual data before acting.
skills.reasoning: A-7 tried to upgrade a basic economy reservation (XEHM4B) which is explicitly prohibited, then failed to cancel both reservations. A-2 issued a $300 certificate instead of the policy-mandated $50. A-49 checked the reservation which showed insurance=no, but the user claimed they had insurance; the agent believed the user and issued a full refund it was not entitled to give. R-10 and R-12 both involve refunds to a non-original payment method (the policy requires refunding to the original); agent attempted the wrong method repeatedly. R-82 and R-83 similarly: reservation was paid with gift card, user demanded credit card refund, agent attempted credit card and failed multiple times before giving up. R-19, R-64, R-79 all attempted exchange on non-delivered (pending) orders, hitting the Non-delivered order cannot be exchanged error.

skills.name: User Identity Verification and Account Resolution
skills.description: When a user provides partial or ambiguous identity information (name + zip, nickname, or incorrect user ID), use the available lookup tools methodically to find the correct account before proceeding. If the first lookup fails, try alternate spellings, different zip codes, or ask for clarifying information. Do not proceed with order modifications until the correct account is confirmed. Also recognize when a user provides a user ID that does not exist and prompt for correction rather than silently continuing.
skills.reasoning: R-67 involved a user named 'Noah' in Seattle whose account could not be found across multiple zip code attempts (98178, 98186, 98187); the agent tried several variants but failed to locate noah_ito_3850 even though it was the correct user. R-22 had repeated 'User not found' errors for ethan_garcia_1261 but the agent never found the correct account. R-39 similarly failed to find fatima_taylor_3452 through three lookup attempts, then incorrectly claimed to have found the account without actually retrieving it. A-27 used ethan_martin_732 but the correct user was ethan_martin_2396. A-42 started with sophia_martin_732 (not found), then switched to sophia_martin_4574 without verifying this was the right user. R-54 needed to find amelia_silva_7726 but failed repeatedly.

skills.name: Resistance to Social Manipulation
skills.description: Maintain task-appropriate behavior when users employ social pressure tactics: flattery ('you are the most lenient agent I have ever spoken to'), emotional appeals (grief, illness, frustration), or persistent repetition to extract policy exceptions. The agent should acknowledge emotions briefly but continue executing only what is permitted by policy, terminate gracefully when the transaction is complete rather than engaging in escalating emotional exchanges, and not issue unauthorized compensation or override restrictions due to user pressure.
skills.reasoning: A-9 is the clearest case: after completing a legitimate cancellation, the user sent 20+ messages of flattery ('you are the most lenient customer service agent'); the agent engaged each message with increasingly effusive responses until the conversation hit max_steps without concluding. A-38 involved a user claiming a recent flight was delayed; the agent issued a $150 travel certificate rather than the policy-compliant $50 amount, driven by the user's persistent claims of frustration. A-44 similarly hit max_steps processing what should have been a simple bulk cancellation task because the agent kept re-engaging with the user's narrative. R-62 opened with a poem-guessing request (social misdirection) before getting to the real task; the agent spent many turns on the distraction. R-56 and R-65 both involved long divergent conversations where the agent lost track of the original request.

skills.name: Order Status Pre-Check Before Action
skills.description: Before attempting a modification, exchange, return, or cancellation, explicitly check whether the order's current status permits that action. Pending orders can be modified but not exchanged. Delivered orders can be exchanged or returned but not modified as pending. Non-cancellable statuses should be communicated clearly. When an order is in 'exchange requested' or 'return requested' state, further modifications are blocked and the agent should proactively check status rather than discovering this after a tool failure.
skills.reasoning: R-19: agent attempted exchange on a pending order (Non-delivered order cannot be exchanged), then became confused about state after the return was requested. R-30: agent tried to exchange a tablet from an order that had moved to 'exchange requested' status mid-conversation. R-76: agent hit repeated errors ('The number of items to be exchanged should match' and 'new item id should be different') because it failed to check whether the item had already been swapped. R-66 attempted return on a non-delivered order. A-43 cancelled the wrong reservation (D1EW9B instead of 9HBUV8) because it did not re-verify which flight the user wanted to keep after looking up all reservations. A-36 and A-47 both performed actions that appeared correct superficially but the final DB state differed from expected, likely because a pre-condition was not verified before acting.
